title: Parallel Corpus Analysis of Text and Audio Comprehension
publisher: Journal of Medical Internet Research / original authors
section_locator: Ahmed et al., JMIR 2025 27:e69772; Methods 178–205; results 209–221; correlations Tables 2–5 (229–346); limitations 366–373; license 448–461
observations: Different presentations of health texts were evaluated for perceived difficulty, multiple-choice/true-false comprehension, and free recall. Text outperformed default TTS audio on comprehension; readability formulas failed to predict comprehension in studied materials, while some had modest associations with free recall, including audio SMOG.
design_and_data: n=487 retained participants (text n=274, audio n=213); US Amazon Mechanical Turk, self-selection after hearing screen; parallel audio/text conditions; audio made with Azure TTS default US male voice/rate and no tuned pauses; stimulus document collections BMJ Lay n=193, WebMD n=40, patient instructions n=40, Simple Wikipedia n=243, BMJ journal n=200. Questions: 2 MC, 2 TF, recall, perceived Likert. BMJ journal MC/TF 76% text vs 58% audio (18 pp); patient instructions 86% vs 66% (20 pp); WebMD 75% vs 55% (20 pp); BMJ Lay 72% vs 69% (3 pp). Comprehension significant across corpora per authors. Perceived difficulty difference null for WebMD and patient instructions. Free-recall exact matching significant for patient instructions and BMJ; semantic recall only BMJ. Audio SMOG exact/similar recall r=-0.12/-0.14 significant; SMOG/audio comprehension r=-0.05 null. No standardized d or causal script effect reported in read sections.
limitations: Most English-speaking-home sample; ~67% male, >94% White; TTS default voice not natural human VO; audio without video/visual cues; self-selected tasks; limited health domain, US crowd workers; question generation by GPT-4 expert-checked. Between-person allocation randomization not explicitly established; correlational text-feature analyses are not interventions. Recall retention is NOT YouTube watch retention.
license_rights: Open access Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; cite authors, article, journal and DOI. Third-party examples/supplements should still be screened.

title: Measure key moments for audience retention
evidence_type: Official platform measurement definitions / analytics guidance
section_locator: YouTube Help retention report lines 17–78 and 114–123
observations: The retention report is at per-video, owner-facing analytics; first-30-second intro, top moments, spikes and dips are descriptive patterns. Spikes can mean rewatching or confusion, dips include skipping or quitting, and changing title/intro is an experimentation suggestion, not evidence of a causal lift. Segmentation can compare new/returning, subscribed/non, paid/organic.
design_and_data: No released source-level dataset, randomization, impact CI or public comparators; key moments for videos >=60s and >=100 views if detected; report processing typically 1–2 days.
limitations: Content, title, thumbnail, recommendations, traffic mix, viewer demographics, duration and editing covary; retention graphs alone cannot attribute causes; 30 seconds is a report definition not mandatory script hook timing.
license_rights: Google/YouTube Help protected material; link and brief analytical summary only; channel-owner analytics access needed for individual curves.
